speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me exactly when the baby was born and how long it has been since they failed to pass meconium? Also, has the baby had any episodes of bilious vomiting since birth?

speaker: Patient
text: 2-day-old male infant. The infant was born via a home birth without complications. The mother reports that the infant has had bilious vomiting and has not been able to pass meconium since birth. She also notes that the infant's abdomen appears distended.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that information. Has the infant passed any stool at all since birth, and have you noticed any blood mixed in with the vomit or stool? Additionally, can you describe the nature of the abdominal distension—is it soft and tympanitic, or does it feel firm and tense to the touch?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Bilious vomiting. I also have Inability to pass meconium, Abdominal distension.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Abdominal_X-ray: Dilated loops of bowel with no gas in the rectum, suggestive of a distal obstruction. Sweat_Test: NORMAL READINGS. IMAGES: No imaging data provided.

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal sweat test rules out cystic fibrosis, so we are looking at a structural or functional obstruction like Hirschsprung disease. Was the baby born with any other congenital anomalies, such as heart defects or umbilical hernias, and is there a family history of thyroid issues or developmental delays?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Newborn, no prior medical history. Birth was uneventful. Social history: The infant is the first child of the family. No known family history of genetic or congenital diseases.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the distal obstruction on X-ray and normal sweat test, Hirschsprung disease is the leading suspect. To confirm this, I need to assess for other associated conditions and check for specific signs; has the baby had any episodes of explosive stool after rectal examination, and are there any other congenital anomalies like cardiac defects or imperforate anus?

speaker: Patient
text: The infant shows signs of distress, possibly due to abdominal discomfort.

speaker: Doctor
text: The clinical picture of delayed meconium passage, bilious vomiting, and distal obstruction with a normal sweat test strongly points to Hirschsprung disease. I will proceed with the definitive diagnostic test. REQUEST TEST: Rectal_Biopsy

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Rectal_Biopsy: Histopathology shows absence of ganglion cells in the submucosa and myenteric plexus, consistent with Hirschsprung’s disease.

speaker: Doctor
text: The rectal biopsy confirms the absence of ganglion cells, which is the definitive diagnostic criterion for this condition. DIAGNOSIS READY: Hirschsprung disease
